summary: Describes Hierarchical Service Function Chaining, an experimental architecture that lets an organization split a large network into multiple administrative domains. The aim is to make large networks easier to design and control and to support independent functional groups.

plainLanguage.summary: Service function chaining sends traffic through a chosen list of network functions, such as firewalls or address translators. This RFC describes how to apply that in a very large network by splitting the network into smaller areas, each run by its own team, with a boundary node that passes traffic between the areas.

questions: how to scale service function chaining
subtitle: Hierarchical decomposition of large networks using service function chaining.

tldr.problem: Service function chaining is hard to run across a large, geographically spread network with many hosts, many forwarding elements and several operating teams, because a single control plane would have to manage every complete path.
tldr.mechanism: The network is split into subdomains, each with its own control plane, and a new node called an Internal Boundary Node bridges the levels, acting as a service function above and a classifier below.
tldr.outcome: The document identifies and analyzes five ways for the boundary node to restore a packet's upper-level path when it leaves the subdomain, and does not pick one, because it was published to collect implementation and deployment experience.

facts.label: Boundary node role above
facts.value: Acts as an SFC-aware service function

facts.label: Boundary node role below
facts.value: Acts as a classifier and the end of the local chain

facts.label: Repurposable context header space
facts.value: 32 bits of the NSH MD Type 0x1 Fixed-Length Context Header

today: RFC 8459 is an Experimental RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated. The document was published to collect implementation and deployment experience, and it deliberately does not recommend one way for the boundary node to join the levels together, because the choices depend on deployment details it leaves open.

sections.title: Decomposing a Large Chaining Network
sections.content:
Service Function Chaining (SFC) is a technique for prescribing differentiated traffic-forwarding policies within an SFC-enabled domain. The SFC architecture is described in detail in RFC 7665 and is not repeated here.

This document focuses on the difficult problem of implementing SFC across a large, geographically dispersed network, potentially comprised of millions of hosts and thousands of network-forwarding elements, and which may involve multiple operational teams with varying functional responsibilities. Some stateful Service Functions (SFs) require bidirectional traffic for transport-layer sessions, for example NATs and firewalls, so some Service Function Paths need to be selected on the basis of transport-layer coordinate stickiness, typically the 5-tuple of source IP address, source port number, destination IP address, destination port number and transport protocol, to specific stateful SF instances.

Difficult problems are often made easier by decomposing them in a hierarchical manner. Instead of a single SFC control plane that can manage, create, withdraw and supervise complete SFPs from one end of the network to the other, the network is decomposed into smaller domains operated by as many SFC control plane components under the same administrative entity. Each subdomain may support a subset of the network applications or a subset of the users. Decomposing a network should be done with care to ease monitoring and troubleshooting of the network and services as a whole, and the criteria for decomposing a domain are deployment specific and beyond the scope of this document.

The document assumes the SFC-aware nodes use the Network Service Header (NSH) (RFC 8300) or a similar labeling mechanism, and that the SFC-enabled domains are under the control of a single organization, so that there is a strong trust relationship between them. Domains operated by different organizations are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Service function chaining sends traffic through a chosen list of network functions, such as firewalls or address translators. This RFC describes how to apply that in a very large network by splitting the network into smaller areas, each run by its own team, with a boundary node that passes traffic between the areas.

sections.title: The Upper Level and the Subdomains
sections.content:
A hierarchy has multiple levels. The topmost level encompasses the entire network domain to be managed, and lower levels encompass portions of the network. The top-level network domain includes SFC data plane components distributed over a wide area: classifiers, Service Function Forwarders (SFFs) and subdomains.

Top-level SFPs carry packets from classifiers through a set of SFFs and subdomains, with the operations within subdomains being opaque to the upper levels. The system is expected to include a top-level control plane responsible for configuring forwarding policies and traffic-classification rules. That control plane manages end-to-end service chains and associated service function paths from network edge points to subdomains, and configures top-level classifiers at a coarse level, for example based on source or destination host, to forward traffic along paths that will transit across appropriate subdomains. It does not configure traffic-classification rules or forwarding policies within the subdomains.

At the network-wide level, the number of SFPs required is a linear function of the number of ways a packet has to traverse different subdomains and egress the network. The various paths that may be followed within a subdomain are not represented by distinct network-wide SFPs; specific policies at the ingress nodes of each subdomain bind flows to subdomain paths.

Packets are classified at the edge of the network to select the paths by which subdomains are to be traversed. At the ingress of each subdomain, packets are reclassified to paths directing them to the required SFs of that subdomain. At the egress of each subdomain, packets are returned to the top-level paths. Some SFs require bidirectional symmetry of paths, so the classifiers at the top level must be configured with policies ensuring outgoing packets take the reverse path of incoming packets through subdomains.

Each subdomain is likely to have a control plane that can operate independently of the top-level control plane, managing classification and forwarding paths within the subdomain, with the details being opaque to the upper-level control elements. The subdomain control plane configures the classification rules in the Internal Boundary Node, where the SFC encapsulation of the top-level domain is converted to and from the SFC encapsulation of the lower-level domain, and configures the forwarding rules in the SFFs of the subdomain. If desired, the pattern can be applied recursively, so that a service function inside a subdomain can itself be a subdomain.
sections.plainLanguage: The top of the hierarchy decides which parts of the network traffic should cross, without knowing what happens inside them. Each subdomain then decides for itself how to route traffic through its own service functions. Traffic is classified again on the way into a subdomain and handed back to the top level on the way out.

sections.title: The Internal Boundary Node
sections.content:
The Internal Boundary Node, or IBN, is responsible for bridging packets between upper and lower layers of SFC-enabled domains. It behaves as an SF to the upper level and looks like a classifier and end of chain to the lower level.

To achieve the benefits of hierarchy, the IBN should apply fine-grained traffic-classification rules at a lower level than the traffic passed to it, so the number of SFPs within the lower level is greater than the number of SFPs arriving at the IBN. The IBN is also the termination of lower-level SFPs, because the packets exiting them must be returned to the upper-level SFPs and forwarded to the next hop in the upper-level domain.

When different metadata schemes are used at different levels, the IBN has further responsibilities. When packets enter the subdomain, it translates upper-level metadata into lower-level metadata, and when packets leave the subdomain at the termination of lower-level SFPs, it translates lower-level metadata back into upper-level metadata. Appropriately configuring IBNs is key to ensuring the consistency of the overall SFC operation, and classification rules, or the lack of them, in the IBN classifier can impact upper levels.

At the start of a chain, the IBN classifier parses incoming packets for IP and transport-layer coordinates such as TCP and UDP, and applies the classification rules given by the subdomain control plane to select a lower-level path. The Service Path Identifier (SPI) and Service Index (SI) are re-marked according to that path. At the end of a lower-level chain, the IBN removes the SFC header and hands the packet back to the SFFs of the upper level.
sections.plainLanguage: The boundary node is the point where one level hands traffic to the next. Above it, it looks like one service function in a chain. Below it, it looks like the classifier that picks the local path and the place where the local chain ends.

sections.title: Five Ways to Restore the Upper-Level Path
sections.content:
When packets leave the subdomain at the end of a lower-level SFP, they have to be restored to their original upper-level SFP. The document identifies five methods, and describes the advantages and drawbacks of each.

  • Flow-stateful IBN. The IBN parses the encapsulated packets for IP and transport-layer coordinates when they arrive, and creates state indexed by some or all of those coordinates, typically source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port and transport protocol. The state holds at least the critical fields of the encapsulating SFC header, namely SPI, SI, MD Type and flags, and may also hold metadata and TTL. When the packet returns, the header is removed, the packet is parsed again for flow-identifying information, and the state is looked up. State cannot be created by packets arriving from the lower-level chain, so packets for which no state can be found must be dropped. This approach cannot be used with SFs that modify the transport coordinates, such as NATs, or that create packets for new coordinates, such as an HTTP cache retrieving content on behalf of the original flow.
  • Encoding upper-level paths in metadata. The IBN pushes the upper-level SPI and SI, or an encoding of them, into a metadata field of the lower-level encapsulation, for example the NSH metadata, and restores them from the packet on the way out. This requires the SFs in the path to be able to forward the metadata and to attach it to any packets they inject. A new metadata header may inflate the packet size when variable-length metadata, MD Type 0x2, is used. Where the MD Type 0x1 Fixed-Length Context Header is not all relevant to the lower-level domain, 32 bits of it could be repurposed within the lower-level domain and restored on leaving.
  • Unique paths per upper-level path. Paths within the subdomain are constrained so that a subdomain SPI unambiguously indicates the egress SPI and SI of the upper domain, and the original path information is restored from a look-up table keyed by the subdomain SPI. The downside is that the number of paths in the lower-level domain is multiplied by the number of upper-level paths that traverse it, so the number of paths grows exponentially as the hierarchy becomes deep. It also requires both levels to use the same metadata configuration, and it does not allow anything to be hidden from the upper level, such as TTL modifications made inside the subdomain.
  • Nesting upper-level NSH within lower-level NSH. The IBN pushes a new NSH header in front of the original one, so that the Lower-NSH header used for forwarding in the lower-level domain precedes the Upper-NSH header from the top-level domain. Traffic with this stack is forwarded according to the Lower-NSH header, while the Upper-NSH header is preserved but not used for forwarding. At the last SFF of the lower-level chain, the Lower-NSH header is removed and the packet is forwarded by the IBN using the Upper-NSH header. The benefit is that no state is needed and all header fields, including flags and TTL, are easily restored. The downside is that SFC-aware SFs in the lower-level domain must be able to parse multiple NSH layers, and the extra overhead may lead to fragmentation or a reduced MTU.
  • Stateful and metadata hybrid. The IBN saves the upper-domain encapsulation under a unique identifier, an hSFC Flow ID, placed for example in the NSH Fixed-Length Context Header field or encoded as a Variable-Length Context Header field when MD Type 0x2 is used. On exit the IBN uses the Flow ID to retrieve the right NSH encapsulation and then strips the Context Header. It works with SFs that change IP addresses or port numbers, does not require all domains to share a metadata scheme, can restore any upper-domain information including metadata, flags and TTL, and needs only one item of metadata in the lower level. Its drawbacks are those of the other stateful approaches, plus the possibility of many unique encapsulations consuming a lot of memory.
sections.plainLanguage: When traffic comes back out of a subdomain, the boundary node has to remember which top-level path it was on. The RFC lists five ways to do that: keep a note keyed by the connection, carry a note in the packet's metadata, use a separate local path for every top-level path, stack a second header in front of the first, or keep a note under a short identifier carried in the packet. Each way trades memory, header size and complexity against the others.

sections.title: Service Index, TTL and the Control Plane
sections.content:
Because the IBN acts as an SFC-aware SF to the upper-level domain, it must decrement the Service Index in the NSH headers of the upper-level path. This should be done when the packet is first received by the IBN, before applying any of the path-restoring strategies, immediately prior to classification.

The NSH base header contains a TTL field, and there is a choice. A subdomain may appear as a pure service function, which should not decrement the TTL from the perspective of the upper-level domain, or all of the TTL changes within the subdomain may be visible to the upper-level domain. Some readers may recognize this as a choice between the pipe and uniform models respectively. The network operator should be given control of this behavior, choosing whether to expose the lower-level topology to the upper layer, and an implementation may support per-packet policy, allowing some users to perform a layer-transcending trace route. The choice affects whether the path-restoring methods restore a saved version of the TTL or propagate it with the packet. The unique-paths method does not permit topology hiding; the other four have their own ways of restoring a saved TTL.

On the control plane, the document sets out expectations. Each control-plane instance manages a single level of the hierarchy of a single domain. Each control plane is agnostic about other levels of the hierarchy, which allows humans to reason about the system within a single domain and control-plane algorithms to use only domain-local inputs: top-level control does not need visibility into subdomain policies, and subdomain control does not need visibility into upper-level policies, with the top level treating a subdomain as though it were an SF. Subdomain control planes are also agnostic about the control planes of other subdomains, so both humans and machines can manipulate subdomain policy without considering the policies of other domains. In this view, it is the IBN that glues the layers together. These expectations do not prohibit network-wide control; a control hierarchy can distribute information to multiple domains and subdomains, but control hierarchy is outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The boundary node must step down the index that says where in the chain a packet is, and the operator chooses whether the top level can see the delay the subdomain adds. Each level of the hierarchy runs its own control plane and does not need to know how the other levels work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
hSFC uses the service chaining architecture, so it inherits the security considerations described in RFC 7665, and it also inherits the security considerations of the data-plane protocols, such as NSH, and the control-plane protocols used to realize the solution. hSFC adheres to the same security considerations as RFC 8300.

The document describes systems that may be managed by distinct teams that all belong to the same administrative entity. Subdomains must have consistent configurations in order to properly forward traffic, so any protocol designed to distribute those configurations must be secure from tampering, and the means of preventing attacks from within a network must be enforced, for example by continuously monitoring the network to detect misbehaviour. All of the systems and protocols must be secure from modification by untrusted agents.

The options that store a context header to bind a flow to its upper-level SFP strip that header before the packet exits the subdomain, and the guards against leaking unwanted context information when entering and exiting a subdomain are described in the section on adapting to NSH-unaware service functions. Control-plane security considerations are left to the corresponding control specification documents.

The document also warns that distributing policies among multiple domains may lead to forwarding loops. NSH supports the ability to detect loops, but the means of ensuring the consistency of the policies should be enabled at all levels of a domain, and within hSFC it is the responsibility of the Control Elements at all levels to prevent such loops.
sections.plainLanguage: Each area of the network is run by its own team, so the settings that are sent between areas must not be tampered with. The document also warns that handing policies between areas can create forwarding loops, and that it is the job of the control software at every level to prevent them.

viz.caption: THE FIVE WAYS TO RESTORE THE UPPER-LEVEL PATH

items.title: Flow state
items.text: Look up the saved path by the connection's addresses and ports. Does not survive a function that rewrites them.

items.title: Metadata
items.text: Carry the upper-level path in the packet's metadata field. Needs functions that preserve metadata.

items.title: Unique local paths
items.text: Give every upper-level path its own local path. The number of local paths grows quickly with depth.

items.title: Nested headers
items.text: Put a second NSH header in front of the first. Costs header size on every packet.

items.title: Flow ID
items.text: Store the path under a short identifier carried in the packet. Costs memory in the boundary node.
